site.name: Positive
site.intro: Five small retellings from India’s living story traditions. Read one, then return to your day a little lighter.

stories.title: The Wisdom of Mahā-Ummagga
stories.source: Mahā-Ummagga-Jātaka (No. 546), The Jataka, Vol. VI, tr. E. B. Cowell and W. H. D. Rouse (1907)
body: In the city of Takkasilā, the young Brahmin Mahā-Ummagga mastered every art and rose to serve King Vedeha of Mithilā as royal chaplain. A jealous courtier laid a cruel wager, betting his own head that Mahā-Ummagga could never unravel three riddles no one had solved before.

Rather than despair, Mahā-Ummagga set out humbly as an ascetic and journeyed to Benares, where the city's sages shared with him their quiet truths. He returned to court and gave each answer without ever speaking the riddles aloud, astonishing the king and earning the revenue of the four gates.

His wisdom later preserved peace and plenty for Mithilā when a borderland king threatened war. The courtier paid his forfeit, and at the close of a life well used, Mahā-Ummagga turned his heart toward the supreme knowledge, a gentle dawn after a long and worthy road.

stories.title: The Gift That Brought Them Home
stories.source: Vessantara-Jātaka (No. 547), The Jataka, Vol. VI, tr. E. B. Cowell and W. H. D. Rouse (1907)
body: In the city of Jetuttara, Prince Vessantara of the Sivi kingdom was renowned for his boundless charity. When drought-stricken Brahmins from Kalinga came begging for the sacred white elephant that brought the rains, he gave it freely, though the whole realm protested. To calm unrest, King Sanjaya banished his son to the forest, where Vessantara went willingly with his wife Maddi and their two small children.

Deep in the wilderness, a Brahmin named Jujaka demanded his children as servants, and another asked for Maddi herself. One by one, Vessantara offered them up, and the very earth trembled at the merit of a heart that held nothing back. Even the gods watched from above, and Sakka, king of the heavens, quietly set in motion a plan to undo the sorrow.

Soon Sakka arranged a joyful reunion of husband, wife, and children. The people of Jetuttara poured out with garlands to welcome them home, and Vessantara returned to his father's kingdom to reign in peace, his giving crowned at last with the warmth of those he loved.

stories.title: Wisdom Wins the Day
stories.source: Vidhurapaṇḍita-Jātaka (No. 545), The Jataka, Vol. VI, tr. E. B. Cowell and W. H. D. Rouse (1907)
body: In the lakeside city of Kālacampā, four old companions now reigned as kings: Sakka of the gods, Varuṇa the Naga king, the Supaṇṇa king, and Dhanañjaya of the Kuru court. When each boasted that his own virtue—patience, forbearance, gentleness, or unhindered mind—was supreme, they agreed to lay the dispute before the wise minister Vidhura-paṇḍita.

Vidhura listened to every verse and answered gently that no single virtue could stand alone. Like spokes fitted to the nave of a wheel, all four qualities must meet in one person before he can rightly be called an ascetic. The kings rejoiced, and Sakka, the Supaṇṇa, Varuṇa, and Dhanañjaya showered him with heavenly silk, a golden garland, a jewel, and a thousand cows with sixteen villages.

Later, when the Naga queen Vimalā's trickery led the Yakkha general Puṇṇaka to carry Vidhura away, the sage's quiet wisdom converted both Puṇṇaka and the whole Naga household. Returned unharmed to Kālacampā with every gift still in his hands, Vidhura walked home as proof that patient understanding can disarm even the fiercest of worlds.

stories.title: Rama-pandita's Calm Return Home
stories.source: Dasharatha Jataka (No. 461), The Jataka, Vol. IV, tr. W. H. D. Rouse (Cowell ed., 1901)
body: In the green folds of the Himalaya, Rama-pandita, his brother Prince Lakkhaṇa, and their sister Lady Sita made a humble hermitage their home. Twelve years stretched ahead, but the eldest brother sat in steady meditation while the younger two gathered wild fruits and lotus blooms from the forest paths.

When the old king passed in the ninth year, Prince Bharata came carrying the five emblems of sovereignty, begging his elder brother to come home. At the pond's edge, Rama-pandita gently led Lakkhaṇa and Sita into the cool water before telling them of their father's death, so the ripples might steady their hearts.

The siblings wept together, then walked back to Benares with Bharata in a procession of quiet grace. There, beneath the white royal umbrella held aloft, calm Rama-pandita was raised at last to the throne that had always awaited him.

stories.title: Prince Ghata's Light in Prison
stories.source: Ghata-Jātaka (No. 355), The Jataka, Vol. III, tr. H. T. Francis and R. A. Neil (Cowell ed., 1897)
body: In the days when Brahmadatta ruled Benares, his son Prince Ghata returned from Takkasilā and governed with a gentle hand. But a scheming minister, cast out for wrongdoing, took refuge with King Vaṅka of Sāvatthi and whispered him toward war. Vaṅka marched on Benares, claimed the city, and bound the prince in heavy chains within a dark prison cell.

Ghata settled into deep meditation and, to the wonder of all, floated cross-legged above the floor. When Vaṅka, his own body burning with fever, came to gloat, he saw the prisoner's face shining like a polished golden mirror. He asked how anyone could smile while others wept, and Ghata answered that grief only robs what cannot be changed, and a soul set free has nothing to fear on land or sea, in village or forest.

So struck was Vaṅka by this quiet radiance that he begged forgiveness, returned Benares to its rightful prince, and went his way in peace. The Bodhisatta entrusted the kingdom to his ministers, withdrew to the cool slopes of the Himālayas, and there, as an ascetic, entered the deep meditation that lifts the heart to the world of Brahmā.
